although such respondents or parties may not have filed any appeal or objection [and may, where there have been decrees in cross-suits or where two or more decrees are passed in one suit, be exercised in respect of all or any of the decrees, although an appeal may not have been filed against such decrees]:

In case of a Slander, the publication takes place, when the words are heard by someone else other than the Plaintiff as well as when the statement is perceived in a defamatory sense, leading to possibility of framing an opinion about the reputation of the person, about whom the statement is made.

the aforesaid process is that the words must be heard by some one else, other than the Plaintiff.

Even if there is no evidence in the affirmative, on behalf of the Respondents,
the initial onus was upon the Appellant/Plaintiff to prove the factum of defamation.
The Defendant cannot prove in the negative that he has not said the words and this part has to be first proven by the Plaintiff in the affirmative.
The Plaintiff's evidence is only limited to the averments by the Plaintiff herself that the slander was made in presence of her family members and in presence of Sarla and Kuldeep.
The pleadings and evidence do not spell out the name/detail or identities of the family members.
The Appellant/Plaintiff in the plaint or examination-in-chief or in her cross examination does not mention the details of the Sarla and Kuldeep beyond their names.
She terms them to be her neighbours, however she is not aware of their addresses.

In terms of Section 60 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872, it is the cardinal rule of evidence that the oral evidence, in all cases, must be direct.

Section 60 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 is reproduced hereinbelow:
"60.
Oral evidence must be direct.

Provided also that, if oral evidence refers to the existence or condition of any material thing other than a document, the Court may, if it thinks fit, require the production of such material thing for its inspection."

sentences.text: Page No. 16 of 18 Thus in terms of Section 60 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872, if oral evidence is required to be given about a fact being heard, being perceived or opinion expressed about it, it has to be of the person who has heard it or perceived it or expressed the opinion about it.
The Plaintiff's oral testimony would not be the direct evidence of the aforesaid words, heard by people other than her and the witnesses were required to be examined.
Therefore, merely the Plaintiff's statement, about the defamatory words, being heard by other person(s) is alone not sufficient, in absence of the testimony of the other person.

Since no witness other than the Plaintiff has been examined,
therefore, the Plaintiff has failed to prove defamation, as it is understood in the terms of law.
The Plaintiff has further sought Rs.1,00,000/- as damages, however the aforesaid amount is not quantified in the plaint nor have the aforesaid damages been proven in the evidence by her.

However the aforesaid aspect becomes immaterial, once the factum of legal defamation has not been proved by the Plaintiff.
7. Order
The Appellant has filed the civil suit for compensation for slander after expiry of prescribed period of limitation.
Further, the Appellant has failed to make out a case of legal civil defamation.

Therefore, no interference is warranted with the judgment and decree of the Court of Ld. Civil ________________________________________________________________ ANIL Kiran Devi Vs. Rajbir Singh & Anr. Page No. 17 of 18 CHANDHEL judge.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The aforesaid words are actionable in themselves, taking into consideration the nature and degree of imputations made.
Therefore the suit has been filed by the Appellant after expiry of the prescribed period of limitation.
The documents relied upon or exhibited by the Plaintiff do not prove or relate to the incident dated 12.12.2016.
In case of a Slander, the publication takes place, when the words are heard by someone else other than the Plaintiff as well as when the statement is perceived in a defamatory sense, leading to possibility of framing an opinion about the reputation of the person, about whom the statement is made.
the aforesaid process is that the words must be heard by some one else, other than the Plaintiff.
Even if there is no evidence in the affirmative, on behalf of the Respondents,
the initial onus was upon the Appellant/Plaintiff to prove the factum of defamation.
The Defendant cannot prove in the negative that he has not said the words and this part has to be first proven by the Plaintiff in the affirmative.
The Plaintiff's evidence is only limited to the averments by the Plaintiff herself that the slander was made in presence of her family members and in presence of Sarla and Kuldeep.
The pleadings and evidence do not spell out the name/detail or identities of the family members.
The Appellant/Plaintiff in the plaint or examination-in-chief or in her cross examination does not mention the details of the Sarla and Kuldeep beyond their names.
In terms of Section 60 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872, it is the cardinal rule of evidence that the oral evidence, in all cases, must be direct.
The Plaintiff's oral testimony would not be the direct evidence of the aforesaid words, heard by people other than her and the witnesses were required to be examined.
Therefore, merely the Plaintiff's statement, about the defamatory words, being heard by other person(s) is alone not sufficient, in absence of the testimony of the other person.
Since no witness other than the Plaintiff has been examined,
therefore, the Plaintiff has failed to prove defamation, as it is understood in the terms of law.
